content: Birth mass refers to the weight of a newborn at the time of delivery. It is closely associated with the gestational age at which the baby is born and can be estimated during pregnancy by measuring the fundal height of the uterus. A baby whose birth weight falls within the normal range for its gestational age is classified as appropriate for gestational age (AGA). Conversely, infants born with a weight either above or below this range often exhibit atypical growth patterns, which may indicate complications during pregnancy that could affect the health of the baby or the mother. The likelihood of a birth mass outside the AGA range is influenced by several factors, including genetic predispositions, the health status of the mother during pregnancy, environmental exposures (such as secondhand smoke), and other circumstances like multiple births, where one or more babies are more likely to fall outside the AGA range. Numerous studies have explored potential associations between birth mass and various health outcomes later in life, such as diabetes, obesity, smoking habits, and intelligence. These studies have yielded varying degrees of success in establishing definitive links. Conditions Associated with Birth Mass Infants may be classified as either large for gestational age (LGA) or small for gestational age (SGA) based on their birth weight relative to their gestational age. Influence on Adult Life Research has investigated how birth mass may influence aspects of an individual's future health and development. The following are some of the key areas of interest: Obesity Infants born at either extreme of the birth weight spectrum (SGA or LGA) are believed to have an increased risk of developing obesity later in life. Growth hormone (GH) therapy at specific doses has been shown to promote catch-up growth in lean body mass (LBM) in some cases. However, GH-treated individuals also experienced a reduction in body fat percentage. Additionally, bone mineral density, as measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA), significantly increased in GH-treated subjects compared to untreated individuals. Despite these findings, there is ongoing debate about whether SGA status has sufficiently adverse effects on children to justify interventions aimed at inducing catch-up growth. Diabetes Infants with low birth mass are thought to have a higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes in adulthood. Intelligence Some studies have demonstrated a direct correlation between higher birth mass and increased intelligence quotient (IQ).
